frontMatter.title: Learning outcomes
intentions: Explain why national averages give an incomplete picture.

completion.description: Review the key notes and explain the concept in your own words.

activities.title: Measuring human wellbeing
activities.lede: The Human Development Index (HDI) helps geographers compare human development.

notes.body: The HDI combines health, education and income. It uses life expectancy at birth; mean and expected years of schooling; and gross national income per person, adjusted for differences in purchasing power.
The index ranges from 0 to 1. A higher value represents higher average achievement in these dimensions, but an average can hide differences within a country.

image.alt: The Human Development Index combines health, education and income into one summary index.
image.caption: HDI brings together three dimensions. It summarises development; it is not a complete picture of wellbeing.
image.rights: Original explanatory diagram for this review prototype; source concepts attributed. No copied source artwork.

keyNotes: HDI combines health, education and income into one index.
Higher HDI values indicate higher average achievement in these dimensions.
National averages can hide inequalities; use other evidence too.

activities.title: What an average can hide
activities.lede: A national summary does not describe every community or individual.

notes.body: People within the same country may have very different opportunities. Compare the national summary with evidence about places and groups before drawing a conclusion about wellbeing.
notes.source: Concept source: UNDP, Human Development Index data centre.

keyNotes: A national average does not show how outcomes are distributed.
Use regional and community evidence alongside national indicators.
